title: Say the good thing
instruction: Notice one thing they handled today that you would normally leave unspoken. Tell them you noticed.
why_it_matters: Small acknowledgements interrupt the tendency to filter familiar effort into the background.

title: Catch the autopilot
instruction: At one ordinary moment together today, notice what each of you does without thinking. Don't change it yet; just name the pattern privately to yourself.
why_it_matters: Noticing a cue-response pattern is the first step toward choosing a different response.

title: One real follow-up
instruction: When they tell you something about their day, ask one genuine follow-up question before talking about your own day.
why_it_matters: A small change in attention can make an ordinary exchange feel less automatic and more responsive.

title: Look up
instruction: The next time they enter the room or meet you somewhere today, pause what you're doing for a few seconds and properly look at them.
why_it_matters: Deliberately shifting attention can interrupt familiar moments that have become almost invisible.

title: Notice the assumption
instruction: The next time something small annoys you, catch the first explanation your mind gives you for why they did it. Don't argue with it; just notice it.
why_it_matters: Automatic interpretations can shape a reaction before we realize an interpretation has happened.

title: Find the detail
instruction: Notice one small detail about your partner today that you haven't paid attention to lately: what they're wearing, doing, reading, humming, or choosing.
why_it_matters: Familiarity can narrow attention. Deliberately noticing detail makes the familiar visible again.

title: Ask beyond logistics
instruction: At some point today, ask one question that isn't about schedules, chores, money, food, or plans.
why_it_matters: Moving one conversation beyond coordination creates a small opening for curiosity.

title: Spot their bid
instruction: Notice one small attempt they make to get your attention today—a comment, joke, photo, question, or look. Respond instead of letting it pass.
why_it_matters: Responding to small bids for attention can change the feel of everyday interaction without requiring a big conversation.

title: Remember the version
instruction: When you see your partner today, briefly remember one thing about them that first drew you in. Keep it to yourself or tell them if it feels natural.
why_it_matters: Bringing an older positive representation to mind can interrupt seeing a familiar person only through today's logistics.

title: Five minutes, no admin
instruction: During five minutes together today, leave chores, schedules, work admin, and tomorrow's planning alone.
why_it_matters: Briefly removing logistical talk creates room for a different kind of interaction.

title: Change the route
instruction: If you walk or drive somewhere together today, take a slightly different route.
why_it_matters: Tiny environmental changes can interrupt autopilot and create fresh shared attention.

title: Choose for each other
instruction: If you get a coffee, snack, or small treat together today, let each person choose for the other within something you both already like.
why_it_matters: A low-stakes change to a familiar choice introduces novelty and attention without requiring a special date.

title: Send the unexpected thing
instruction: Send them something during the day that isn't practical: a photo, thought, joke, or tiny thing that made you think of them.
why_it_matters: Changing a communication channel from coordination to connection adds novelty to an ordinary day.

title: Swap one default
instruction: Pick one tiny default you normally control—music, route, show, side of the sofa, dinner choice—and let them choose today.
why_it_matters: Changing a predictable micro-routine creates a safe behavioral experiment in flexibility.

title: Tiny surprise
instruction: Do one small useful or enjoyable thing they aren't expecting today. Keep it small enough that it doesn't create an obligation to react.
why_it_matters: A low-pressure positive surprise can interrupt predictability while reinforcing attention to the other person.

title: Try their pick
instruction: Choose one low-stakes thing your partner likes that you usually wouldn't pick—song, snack, short video, route, or activity—and join them in it once.
why_it_matters: Trying the other person's preference is a small approach behavior that breaks personal defaults.

title: Turn an errand into ten minutes
instruction: If you're doing an errand together, add ten unplanned minutes: walk one extra block, sit somewhere, or look around without rushing home.
why_it_matters: Adding a small rewarding element to an existing routine is easier than creating a separate event from scratch.

title: No usual seats
instruction: If you're somewhere you visit regularly, sit somewhere different today.
why_it_matters: A tiny environmental change can make a familiar setting more noticeable again.

title: Bring back a song
instruction: Play one song connected to a good shared memory while you're together or send it to them without a long explanation.
why_it_matters: A familiar positive cue can reactivate shared memory while changing the emotional texture of an ordinary moment.

title: Let the phone wait
instruction: Choose one ordinary five-minute moment together today and leave your phone out of reach until the moment is over.
why_it_matters: Changing the environment removes a competing cue and makes attention easier rather than relying on willpower.

title: Make the ordinary invitation
instruction: Instead of automatically doing one normal thing separately today, invite them to join you: a walk, shop run, coffee, cooking, or quick errand.
why_it_matters: An invitation turns an existing routine into an opportunity for shared activity without adding much effort.

title: One new corner
instruction: If you're already out together, spend five minutes somewhere you've never stopped before—a side street, bench, shop, or view.
why_it_matters: Small doses of novelty can make shared time feel less interchangeable.

title: Reverse one role
instruction: For one small routine today, swap who normally does it or who takes the lead.
why_it_matters: Changing a familiar role can expose hidden assumptions and make an automatic division of labor visible.

title: Ask for a micro-adventure
instruction: Offer two tiny options that are different from the usual—walk after dinner or dessert outside, new café or old favorite—and let them pick.
why_it_matters: Constrained choices make novelty easier to act on than vague plans to 'do more together.'

title: Change the first minute
instruction: Pick one recurring moment today—waking up, coming home, dinner, getting into the car—and deliberately change only its first minute.
why_it_matters: Changing the start of a familiar sequence can disrupt the rest of an automatic pattern with very little effort.

title: Add one playful choice
instruction: Turn one boring decision today into a playful one: coin flip the takeaway, each pick a mystery snack, or choose the next song for each other.
why_it_matters: Play introduces positive affect into routines that normally run on efficiency alone.

title: Pause one beat
instruction: The next time you feel yourself giving an automatic sharp, dismissive, or impatient reply, wait one breath before answering.
why_it_matters: A short pause creates room between cue and response, making an alternative behavior possible.

title: What else could it mean?
instruction: If you catch yourself deciding what your partner meant by something today, ask yourself once: 'What else could this mean?' before responding.
why_it_matters: Generating an alternative interpretation can loosen the link between an assumption and an automatic reaction.

title: Finish hearing it
instruction: In one conversation today, wait until they fully finish their point before preparing your answer.
why_it_matters: Shifting attention from reply-planning to listening changes a common automatic conversational pattern.

title: Answer the feeling first
instruction: If they tell you about a frustrating moment today, respond to how it sounds before offering a fix or solution.
why_it_matters: Changing from automatic problem-solving to responsiveness can make the other person feel heard without requiring a long discussion.

title: Lower the volume, not the point
instruction: If a small disagreement appears today, try saying the same point once with a calmer first sentence rather than abandoning the point.
why_it_matters: Changing delivery while keeping the underlying need intact tests whether the interaction pattern can shift without avoidance.

title: Repair the small miss
instruction: If you are unnecessarily short, distracted, or dismissive today, correct it while the moment is still small: 'That came out wrong' or 'Sorry, I wasn't listening.'
why_it_matters: Quick repair prevents a minor automatic response from becoming the tone of the interaction.

title: Change the question
instruction: When you're tempted to ask a loaded question such as 'Why do you always...?', turn it into a concrete request about this moment.
why_it_matters: A specific request reduces mind-reading and global judgments while preserving the underlying need.

title: Don't keep the score once
instruction: Catch one moment today when you're mentally counting who did more. Instead, decide what you actually need and either ask plainly or let this one go.
why_it_matters: Moving from internal scorekeeping to a specific choice interrupts resentment-building without denying genuine imbalance.

title: One generous reading
instruction: For one ambiguous thing your partner does today, deliberately choose the most reasonable non-hostile explanation that still fits the facts.
why_it_matters: Testing a less threatening interpretation can reduce automatic escalation when intent is genuinely unclear.

title: Turn toward once
instruction: If they make a small comment or show you something while you're occupied, give them your full attention for ten seconds before returning to what you were doing.
why_it_matters: A brief deliberate response replaces automatic partial attention with a clear moment of responsiveness.

title: Ask before fixing
instruction: If they bring you a problem today, ask 'Do you want ideas or do you want me to listen?' before choosing your response.
why_it_matters: A simple choice interrupts habitual fixing and makes support more responsive to what is actually wanted.

title: Reset outside
instruction: If the two of you feel stuck in the same mood at home, suggest a ten-minute walk rather than trying to solve the mood in the same room.
why_it_matters: Changing context can interrupt environmental cues that help maintain an unproductive interaction pattern.

title: One different goodbye
instruction: Before one separation today—work, errands, sleep, travel—make the goodbye slightly more intentional than usual: eye contact, a kind sentence, or a proper 'see you later.'
why_it_matters: Recurring transition moments are strong cues for small repeatable changes.

title: Break the text reflex
instruction: If a message from them irritates you today, don't send the first reply you compose. Re-read it once and remove the part you wouldn't say calmly in person.
why_it_matters: A small delay can interrupt rapid interpretation-response loops that are amplified in text.

title: Pick one keeper
instruction: Choose one Move from the last three weeks that genuinely improved a moment between you. Mark that one as worth repeating.
why_it_matters: Selecting a behavior that produced a useful result makes repetition intentional rather than relying on memory.

title: Attach it to a cue
instruction: Take one Keeper and decide exactly when it will happen again: after coffee, when you get home, on the walk to the shop, or before sleep.
why_it_matters: Linking a behavior to an existing recurring cue makes remembering it easier.

title: Make it smaller
instruction: Take a Move you liked but found hard to repeat. Reduce it until it feels almost too easy to skip: twenty minutes becomes five; a big plan becomes one question.
why_it_matters: Reducing friction makes repetition more likely and helps separate the useful behavior from unnecessary effort.

title: Repeat the greeting
instruction: Choose one arrival or reunion today and repeat the intentional greeting you tried earlier: stop, look up, and properly acknowledge each other.
why_it_matters: Repeating a behavior at the same cue strengthens the cue-behavior link.

title: Protect five minutes
instruction: Choose one five-minute window that worked well for you—coffee, after dinner, a walk, before bed—and make it deliberately phone-free again today.
why_it_matters: Repeating a useful environmental setup can turn attention into a routine rather than a daily decision.

title: Keep the outside ritual
instruction: Pick one tiny thing outside the house you could realistically repeat weekly: a walk, coffee stop, market lap, bench, or errand detour. Do it or choose when you'll do it next.
why_it_matters: Attaching connection to an existing place or routine lowers the effort needed to repeat it.

title: Keep the question
instruction: Choose one question that opened a better conversation this month. Ask it again in a new context rather than searching for a brand-new technique.
why_it_matters: Repeating a successful conversational behavior helps turn it into a natural response.

title: Plan for the bad day
instruction: Choose one Keeper and finish this sentence privately: 'Even on a busy or bad day, I can still do the two-minute version by…'
why_it_matters: Planning a minimum version protects a new behavior when motivation and time are low.

title: Make the cue visible
instruction: For one Keeper, change something small in the environment so it reminds you: put the phones away at dinner, leave walking shoes by the door, or add a private calendar cue.
why_it_matters: Environmental prompts reduce the need to remember a new behavior at exactly the right moment.

title: Name what changed
instruction: At the end of today, privately identify one small interaction that feels different from four weeks ago and the behavior that helped create it.
why_it_matters: Connecting a useful outcome to a specific behavior reinforces what is worth carrying forward.
